issues.legal_issue: A conviction cannot be substituted for an acquittal on appeal merely because the appellate court prefers a different view of the same evidence when the trial court’s view was reasonably possible.
material_facts: The trial magistrate acquitted the accused after rejecting the prosecution evidence and identifying problems with the discharge documents.
The High Court reversed the acquittal and convicted the accused on the evidence considered by the magistrate.
The Supreme Court found the magistrate’s view reasonably possible and that the High Court had not displaced the circumstances relied on by the magistrate.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in reversing the acquittal merely because it took a different view of the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal against acquittal, the appellate court may reverse the acquittal only after displacing the circumstances on which the trial court relied; a different view of the same evidence is insufficient if the acquittal represents an equally reasonably possible view. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this principle.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking to overturn an acquittal.
predicates.trial_view_reasonably_possible: The trial court’s assessment of the evidence is a reasonably possible view of the case.
predicates.appellate_court_did_not_displace_trial_r: The appellate court did not displace the circumstances on which the trial court based its acquittal.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal, the trial court’s reasonably possible view must stand if the appellate court has not displaced the reasons supporting it.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for criminal breach of trust cannot stand without reliable evidence that the accused received the money alleged to have been entrusted to them.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that the complainants paid money to the accused in exchange for discharge certificates and that the accused failed to deposit it with the society.

The trial magistrate found no reliable evidence that the payment had been made and found interpolations in the discharge certificates, including additions concerning receipt of money that ran into the accused’s signatures.
The prosecution witnesses who said money was paid relied on memory and had kept no record; the land acquisition officer did not witness the payment.
The debt had previously been written off, and the Supreme Court found no apparent reason for the complainants to make the alleged payment.
The complaint was made about two years after the alleged occurrence without a reasonable explanation for the delay.
issues.conclusion: There was no legal evidence supporting the conviction; the conviction and sentence were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution had to establish the alleged receipt of money to support the claim that it was entrusted and then misappropriated. The unreliable and interpolated documents, unsupported recollections, and surrounding improbabilities did not provide legal evidence for the conviction under Sections 406, 409, or 420 IPC. The judgment cites no earlier cases for this evidentiary conclusion.

predicates.criminal_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a criminal conviction.
predicates.alleged_receipt_is_essential_to_offence: The alleged offence depends on proof that the accused received the property said to have been entrusted or misappropriated.
predicates.no_reliable_evidence_of_receipt: The evidence does not reliably establish that the accused received the property alleged to have been entrusted to them.

issues.definition: In a criminal conviction appeal, if the offence depends on proof of receipt and that receipt is not reliably established, the conviction must be set aside.
